title: Basic Concepts and Stoichiometry

toc.title: 1.1 Atoms, molecules, valency and radicals; relative masses and the atomic mass unit
1.2 Chemical equations, empirical and molecular formulae, percentage composition
1.3 Dalton's atomic theory, the laws of stoichiometry and Avogadro's law
1.4 The mole concept, limiting reactant and percentage yield

html:
This chapter is the arithmetic of chemistry.

It carries about two of the seventeen Physical Chemistry questions in the paper (our estimate from the MEC topic list), but the mole concept it builds is used again in volumetric analysis, equilibrium, electrochemistry and thermodynamics questions — a slip here costs marks several times over.

The questions come in three kinds: a definition or a law with its author, a one-line conversion between mass, moles, particles and gas volume, and a short stoichiometry problem (limiting reactant, percentage yield, empirical formula).

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of one ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g; relative atomic mass has no unit; average atomic mass from isotope abundances.
  • Writing formulae from valencies and radicals, including the awkward ones (Hg₂²⁺, S₂O₃²⁻, Cr₂O₇²⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻).
  • Empirical formula from percentage composition; molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with M = 2 × vapour density.
  • The five laws of chemical combination, their authors and a test example for each; which of Dalton's postulates failed.
  • Avogadro's law — equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules (not atoms); 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP.
  • The one-line conversions n = m/M = N/N_A = V/22.4.
  • Limiting reactant (smallest moles ÷ coefficient) and percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

1.1 Atoms, molecules, valency and radicals; relative masses and the atomic mass unit

Atom, molecule and atomicity

Atom and molecule

An atom is the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction; it may or may not exist independently. A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that can exist independently and shows all the properties of that substance.

The number of atoms in one molecule of an element is its atomicity.

Atomicity Examples Remember
1 (monoatomic) He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; metal vapours (Na, Hg) all noble gases
2 (diatomic) H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ "the seven diatomics"
3 (triatomic) O₃ (ozone) allotrope of oxygen
4 (tetra-atomic) P₄ (white phosphorus), As₄ tetrahedral molecule
8 (polyatomic) S₈ (rhombic and monoclinic sulphur) crown-shaped ring

Valency

Valency is the combining capacity of an element: the number of hydrogen atoms (or chlorine atoms, or twice the number of oxygen atoms) that one atom of it combines with or displaces.

In electronic terms it is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares when it bonds (Unit 4). Several metals show variable valency; the old names use -ous for the lower and -ic for the higher valency.

Element Lower valency (-ous) Higher valency (-ic)
Iron Fe²⁺ ferrous Fe³⁺ ferric
Copper Cu⁺ cuprous Cu²⁺ cupric
Mercury Hg₂²⁺ mercurous (each Hg is +1) Hg²⁺ mercuric
Tin Sn²⁺ stannous Sn⁴⁺ stannic
Lead Pb²⁺ plumbous Pb⁴⁺ plumbic
Gold Au⁺ aurous Au³⁺ auric
Valency is not oxidation number

Valency is a plain number with no sign. Oxidation number carries a sign and can be zero or a fraction.

Carbon has valency 4 in CH₄, CH₂Cl₂ and CCl₄, but its oxidation number is −4, 0 and +4 respectively; in Fe₃O₄ the average oxidation number of iron is +8/3. Oxidation numbers are developed in Unit 5.

Radicals

Radical

A radical is an atom or a group of atoms carrying a charge that behaves as a single unit in chemical reactions. Positive radicals are basic radicals (cations); negative radicals are acid radicals (anions).

Valency Basic radicals Acid radicals
1 Na⁺, K⁺, Ag⁺, Cu⁺, NH₄⁺ (ammonium), H₃O⁺ (hydronium) Cl⁻, OH⁻, NO₃⁻ (nitrate), NO₂⁻ (nitrite), HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate), HSO₄⁻ (bisulphate), CN⁻ (cyanide), CH₃COO⁻ (acetate), MnO₄⁻ (permanganate), ClO₃⁻ (chlorate), ClO⁻ (hypochlorite)
2 Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺ O²⁻, S²⁻, SO₄²⁻, SO₃²⁻ (sulphite), CO₃²⁻, S₂O₃²⁻ (thiosulphate), CrO₄²⁻ (chromate), Cr₂O₇²⁻ (dichromate), C₂O₄²⁻ (oxalate), MnO₄²⁻ (manganate), ZnO₂²⁻ (zincate)
3 Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, Cr³⁺ N³⁻ (nitride), PO₄³⁻ (phosphate), AsO₄³⁻ (arsenate), [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (ferricyanide)
4 Sn⁴⁺, Pb⁴⁺ [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ (ferrocyanide), SiO₄⁴⁻ (orthosilicate)

Writing a formula — criss-cross. Write the basic radical first, swap the valencies into subscripts, cancel any common factor, and bracket a polyatomic radical that is taken more than once: Al³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃; Ca²⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂; Sn⁴⁺ + O²⁻ → Sn₂O₄ → SnO₂; K⁺ + [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ → K₄[Fe(CN)₆]; NH₄⁺ + Cr₂O₇²⁻ → (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇.

Check total positive charge = total negative charge.

Three formulae students get wrong

Mercurous chloride (calomel) is Hg₂Cl₂, not HgCl, because mercury(I) exists as the pair Hg₂²⁺. Ferric sulphate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃ and ferrous sulphate FeSO₄. Hypo (sodium thiosulphate) is Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O — not Na₂SO₃, which is sodium sulphite.

Relative atomic mass, molecular mass and the atomic mass unit

Atomic mass unit and relative atomic mass

One atomic mass unit (u, also called the dalton, Da) is one-twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12: 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

The relative atomic mass of an element is the number of times one atom of the element is heavier than 1/12 of a ¹²C atom. Being a ratio, it has no unit.

A_r = \frac{\text{mass of one atom of the element}}{\frac{1}{12}\times \text{mass of one }^{12}\text{C atom}}

  • Relative molecular mass = sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula (H₂SO₄: 2 + 32 + 64 = 98). For ionic solids, which have no molecules, the same sum is the formula mass (NaCl: 58.5).
  • Gram atomic mass (one gram-atom) and gram molecular mass (one gram-molecule) are the same numbers in grams — that is, the mass of one mole.
  • Standards over time: H = 1 (Dalton) → O = 16 (chemists' scale until 1961) → ¹²C = 12 exactly (IUPAC, 1961, still in use).
  • Because 1 u = (1/N_A) g, 1 g = 6.02 × 10²³ u, and the mass of one particle in grams is M/N_A.

Average atomic mass. Most elements are mixtures of isotopes, so the tabulated atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average: \bar{A} = \sum (\text{fraction} \times \text{isotopic mass}).

For two isotopes there is a faster form — add to the lighter mass the mass difference times the fraction of the heavier isotope.

Average atomic mass in one line

Problem. Copper is 69 % ⁶³Cu and 31 % ⁶⁵Cu. Taking the isotopic masses as 63 and 65, find the average atomic mass of copper.

Solution. Lighter mass + (difference × fraction of heavier) = 63 + 2 × 0.31 = 63 + 0.62 = 63.62 ≈ 63.6. Reverse use: if the average and the two masses are given, the fraction of the heavier isotope is (average − lighter) ÷ (heavier − lighter).

Mass of single particles

Problem. Find the mass in grams of one atom of ¹²C and of one molecule of CO₂ (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

Solution. Mass of one particle = M ÷ N_A. One ¹²C atom: 12 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.99 × 10⁻²³ g (and 1/12 of this is 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g = 1 u). One CO₂ molecule: 44 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g.

1.2 Chemical equations, empirical and molecular formulae, percentage composition

What an equation tells you — and what it does not

A balanced chemical equation is a statement of conservation: the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

A balanced equation tells It does not tell (unless written in)
the reactants and products the rate or time taken (that is kinetics)
the mole ratio of all species the conditions — temperature, pressure, catalyst
the mass ratio (with molar masses) whether the reaction is complete or reversible
the volume ratio of gases at the same T and P the physical states and the concentrations
that atoms (and mass) are conserved the mechanism, or whether it happens at all

An equation is made more informative by writing states (s, l, g, aq), conditions over the arrow, ⇌ for a reversible reaction and ΔH for the heat change: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ (Fe catalyst, about 450 °C, 200 atm).

Balancing by inspection. Balance first the element that appears in the fewest formulae, leave H and O to the end, and balance a free element (O₂, H₂) last; clear any fraction by multiplying through. For any combustion there is a formula worth knowing:

\text{C}_x\text{H}_y\text{O}_z + \left(x + \frac{y}{4} - \frac{z}{2}\right)\text{O}_2 \rightarrow x\,\text{CO}_2 + \frac{y}{2}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}

So propane C₃H₈ needs 3 + 8/4 = 5 O₂; ethanol C₂H₆O needs 2 + 6/4 − 1/2 = 3 O₂; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ needs 6 + 3 − 3 = 6 O₂. Redox equations are balanced in Unit 5.

Percentage composition

\text{mass \% of an element} = \frac{(\text{atoms of it in the formula}) \times A_r}{M} \times 100

Compound M Result worth remembering
H₂O 18 H 11.1 %, O 88.9 % (H : O = 1 : 8 by mass)
CO₂ 44 C 27.3 %
CH₄ 16 C 75 %, H 25 %
Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ 180 C 40.0 %, H 6.7 %, O 53.3 %
Urea CO(NH₂)₂ 60 N 46.7 % — the richest common solid nitrogen fertiliser
NH₄NO₃ 80 N 35.0 %
(NH₄)₂SO₄ 132 N 21.2 %
CuSO₄·5H₂O 249.5 water of crystallisation 36.1 %
Na₂CO₃·10H₂O 286 water of crystallisation 62.9 %

Empirical and molecular formula

Empirical and molecular formula

The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical-formula mass (a whole number).

Method from percentages. (1) Take 100 g, so % becomes grams. (2) Divide by the atomic mass to get relative moles. (3) Divide by the smallest. (4) If a ratio ends in .5, multiply all by 2; in .33 or .67, by 3; in .25 or .75, by 4.

(5) Find n from the molar mass — for a gas or vapour, M = 2 × vapour density.

Empirical formula Compounds sharing it
CH ethyne C₂H₂, benzene C₆H₆
CH₂ ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, cyclohexane C₆H₁₂
CH₂O methanal HCHO, ethanoic acid C₂H₄O₂, glucose C₆H₁₂O₆
CH₃ ethane C₂H₆
HO hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂
NO₂ dinitrogen tetroxide N₂O₄
Molecular formula from percentages

Problem. A hydrocarbon contains 92.3 % C and 7.7 % H; its vapour density is 39. Find its molecular formula.

Solution. C : H = 92.3/12 : 7.7/1 = 7.69 : 7.7 = 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH (mass 13). M = 2 × 39 = 78, so n = 78/13 = 6. Molecular formula C₆H₆ (benzene).

Empirical formula from combustion data

Problem. 0.30 g of an organic compound containing C, H and O burns to give 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O. Find its empirical formula.

Solution. Mass of C = 0.44 × 12/44 = 0.12 g; mass of H = 0.18 × 2/18 = 0.02 g; mass of O = 0.30 − 0.12 − 0.02 = 0.16 g. Moles C : H : O = 0.01 : 0.02 : 0.01 = 1 : 2 : 1. Empirical formula CH₂O.

Percentages that do not add up to 100

If only C and H percentages are given and they add to less than 100, the remainder is oxygen (unless another element is named). And never round 1.5 to 2 or 1.33 to 1 — multiply the whole ratio instead: C : H = 1 : 1.5 means C₂H₃, not CH₂.

1.3 Dalton's atomic theory, the laws of stoichiometry and Avogadro's law

Dalton's atomic theory (1808) and what survived

Postulate Status today
Matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms Failed — atoms contain electrons, protons and neutrons
Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed Holds for chemical change; fails in nuclear reactions
Atoms of one element are identical in mass and properties Failed — isotopes (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl)
Atoms of different elements have different masses Failed — isobars have equal mass numbers (⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca)
Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios Whole numbers yes, but not always simple (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, proteins); fails for non-stoichiometric solids
The atom is the smallest unit taking part in a chemical reaction Still true

The laws of chemical combination

Law (author) Statement Test example
Conservation of mass (Lavoisier) In a chemical change the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants 4 g H₂ + 32 g O₂ → 36 g H₂O
Definite (constant) proportions (Proust) A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed ratio by mass, whatever its source water from the Koshi or from a laboratory: H : O = 1 : 8
Multiple proportions (Dalton) When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio O per 28 g N in N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂, N₂O₅ = 16, 32, 48, 64, 80 → 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5
Reciprocal proportions (Richter) When two elements each combine with a fixed mass of a third, the masses in which they do so are in the same ratio (or a simple multiple of it) as the ratio in which they combine with each other 12 g C takes 4 g H (CH₄) and 32 g O (CO₂): H : O = 1 : 8, the same as in H₂O
Gaseous volumes (Gay-Lussac) Gases react, and gaseous products form, in volumes bearing a simple whole-number ratio, at the same T and P H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl is 1 : 1 : 2 by volume; N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ is 1 : 3 : 2
Where the laws fail — the favourite distractors
  • Conservation of mass fails measurably only in nuclear reactions (E = mc^2); the mass change in a chemical reaction exists but is far too small to weigh.
  • Definite proportions fails for non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds such as Fe₀.₉₅O, and when isotopes differ: H : O by mass is 1 : 8 in H₂O but 1 : 4 in D₂O.
  • Gay-Lussac's law is about gas volumes only; volumes are not conserved (2 vol H₂ + 1 vol O₂ → 2 vol steam), but mass always is.
Testing the law of multiple proportions

Problem. Two oxides of nitrogen contain 63.6 % and 46.7 % nitrogen by mass. Show that they obey the law of multiple proportions.

Solution. Oxygen per 1 g of nitrogen: first oxide 36.4/63.6 = 0.572 g; second oxide 53.3/46.7 = 1.141 g. Ratio 0.572 : 1.141 = 1 : 2, a simple whole-number ratio (the oxides are N₂O and NO).

Avogadro's law and its deductions

Avogadro's law (1811)

Equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.

Avogadro's law reconciled Gay-Lussac's volume ratios with atomic theory.

If hydrogen and chlorine were single atoms, 1 volume + 1 volume would give only 1 volume of HCl; the observed 2 volumes require diatomic molecules: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Its deductions are the working tools of this chapter:

  1. Elementary gases such as H₂, N₂, O₂ and Cl₂ are diatomic.
  2. M = 2 × VD. Vapour density is the mass of a volume of gas divided by the mass of the same volume of hydrogen at the same T and P. Equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, so VD = M(gas)/M(H₂) = M/2.
  3. Molar volume. One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (273 K, 1 atm) — so the density of a gas at STP is M/22.4 g L⁻¹. (At 273 K and 1 bar the molar volume is 22.7 L; at 298 K and 1 atm it is 24.5 L. CEE problems use 22.4 L at STP unless they say otherwise.)
  4. Gas volumes react in the coefficient ratio. At the same T and P, volume ratio = mole ratio, so gas–gas problems need no conversion to moles at all.
Formula of a gas from volumes alone

Problem. 10 mL of a gaseous hydrocarbon needs exactly 30 mL of O₂ for complete combustion and gives 20 mL of CO₂, all volumes at the same T and P. Find its formula.

Solution. For CₓHᵧ, volumes are in the ratio 1 : (x + y/4) : x. CO₂: x = 20/10 = 2. O₂: x + y/4 = 30/10 = 3, so y = 4. The gas is C₂H₄ (ethene).

Equal volumes, not equal atoms

1 L of He and 1 L of O₃ at the same T and P contain the same number of molecules, but the ozone contains three times as many atoms and twelve times the mass (48 against 4).

1.4 The mole concept, limiting reactant and percentage yield

The mole

Mole (SI, 2019)

The mole is the amount of substance that contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons…). This number is the Avogadro constant, N_A.

Before 2019 the mole was defined as the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12 — numerically the same.

The molar mass M (g mol⁻¹) has the same number as the relative molecular mass. Every conversion goes through moles:

n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V_{\text{gas at STP}}}{22.4\ \text{L}}

Counting what is inside. Atoms = moles of molecules × N_A × atomicity. Electrons in a molecule = sum of the atomic numbers (minus the charge for a cation, plus it for an anion).

Useful ten-electron species: H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, HF, Ne, NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, OH⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺. N₂ and CO each have 14 electrons and the same molar mass, 28.

Particles in a mass

Problem. For 4.4 g of CO₂ find the number of molecules, atoms and electrons (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

Solution. n = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol. Molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²². Atoms = 3 × that = 1.81 × 10²³. Electrons: CO₂ has 6 + 8 + 8 = 22, so 22 × 6.02 × 10²² = 1.32 × 10²⁴.

Stoichiometry — the mole-ratio method

  1. Write the balanced equation.
  2. Convert what is given into moles.
  3. Multiply by the coefficient ratio (wanted ÷ given).
  4. Convert the answer into the unit asked for — grams, litres at STP, or particles.

For mass-to-mass problems the steps collapse into one line: mass of B = mass of A × \dfrac{b \times M_B}{a \times M_A}, where a and b are the coefficients.

From CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, 50 g of CaCO₃ (0.5 mol) gives 0.5 × 56 = 28 g CaO and 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 L CO₂ at STP.

For a chain of reactions, follow one atom: in S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄ every sulphur atom ends up in one H₂SO₄, so 32 g of sulphur gives at most 98 g of acid (the principle of atom conservation).

Limiting reactant

Limiting and excess reactant

The limiting reactant is the reactant that is used up first in a reaction; it decides the maximum amount of product. The other reactants are present in excess and are partly left over.

Rule: for each reactant compute moles ÷ its coefficient; the smallest value marks the limiting reactant. All products are calculated from it.

Limiting reactant in ammonia synthesis

Problem. 28 g of N₂ and 9 g of H₂ react, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, until one of them is used up. Which reactant is limiting? What mass of NH₃ forms and what is left over?

Solution. N₂: 28/28 = 1 mol, 1/1 = 1. H₂: 9/2 = 4.5 mol, 4.5/3 = 1.5. N₂ gives the smaller value, so N₂ is limiting. NH₃ = 2 × 1 = 2 mol = 34 g. H₂ used = 3 mol; left = 1.5 mol = 3 g.

Check 28 + 9 = 34 + 3.

"Smaller mass" or "fewer moles" is not the test

In the example above H₂ has the smaller mass (9 g against 28 g), yet N₂ is limiting. And with 2 mol H₂ + 2 mol O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O) the moles are equal, yet H₂ is limiting because its coefficient is 2. Always divide by the coefficient.

Percentage yield and purity

\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100

\text{percentage purity} = \frac{\text{mass of pure substance}}{\text{mass of sample}} \times 100

The theoretical yield is what the limiting reactant would give by the equation. Real yields are lower because of side reactions, reversible or incomplete reaction and losses during separation and purification.

With an impure reactant, first find the mass of the pure substance, then do the stoichiometry.

Percentage yield of fermentation

Problem. Fermentation, C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, of 90 g of glucose gives 36.8 g of ethanol. Find the percentage yield. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

Solution. Glucose = 90/180 = 0.5 mol → theoretical ethanol = 1 mol = 46 g. Yield = 36.8/46 × 100 = 80 %.

Reading the options of a stoichiometry MCQ

Setters build the wrong options from predictable slips: using the coefficient ratio upside down, forgetting the coefficient altogether (a 1 : 1 answer), ignoring purity (the 100 % answer), or adding the masses of both reactants when one is in excess.

If two options differ by exactly your coefficient ratio, recheck that step before choosing.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Relation
Atomic mass unit 1 u = 1/12 × mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g; 1 g = 6.02 × 10²³ u
Average atomic mass Σ (fraction × isotopic mass); two isotopes: lighter + difference × fraction of heavier
Mass of one particle M / N_A grams
Moles n = m/M = N/N_A = V(STP)/22.4 L
Gas density at STP ρ = M/22.4 g L⁻¹
Vapour density M = 2 × VD
Molecular formula n × empirical formula; n = M ÷ empirical-formula mass
Mass % of an element (atoms × A_r)/M × 100
Combustion analysis m(C) = m(CO₂) × 12/44; m(H) = m(H₂O) × 2/18
O₂ for burning CₓHᵧO_z x + y/4 − z/2 mol per mol
Limiting reactant smallest (moles ÷ coefficient)
Yield and purity % yield = actual/theoretical × 100; % purity = pure/sample × 100
Law Author One-line test
Conservation of mass Lavoisier mass of reactants = mass of products (fails only in nuclear change)
Definite proportions Proust fixed mass ratio whatever the source (fails: Fe₀.₉₅O, isotopes)
Multiple proportions Dalton CO/CO₂, H₂O/H₂O₂, SO₂/SO₃, Cu₂O/CuO, the five N oxides
Reciprocal proportions Richter CH₄, CO₂ and H₂O

Equal volumes, equal molecules Avogadro M = 2 VD; 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP

Molar volumes: 22.4 L (273 K, 1 atm, the CEE value) · 22.7 L (273 K, 1 bar) · 24.5 L (298 K, 1 atm). Atomicities: noble gases 1, O₃ 3, P₄ 4, S₈ 8.

Chapter summary

  • 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g; relative atomic and molecular masses are unitless ratios; the tabulated atomic mass is an isotope-weighted average.
  • Formulae come from valencies by criss-cross; learn the radicals with their charges, and remember Hg₂²⁺ (Hg₂Cl₂), S₂O₃²⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻.
  • Percentage of an element = (atoms × A_r)/M × 100; urea is 46.7 % N, CuSO₄·5H₂O is 36.1 % water.
  • Empirical formula: % → ÷ A_r → ÷ smallest → whole numbers; molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with M = 2 × VD.
  • Lavoisier (mass), Proust (definite), Dalton (multiple), Richter (reciprocal), Gay-Lussac (gas volumes), Avogadro (equal volumes, equal molecules).
  • Dalton's indivisibility and identical-mass postulates failed (subatomic particles, isotopes, isobars); conservation of atoms in chemical change survives.
  • One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ entities (exact since 2019) = M grams = 22.4 L of gas at STP; n = m/M = N/N_A = V/22.4.
  • Limiting reactant = smallest moles ÷ coefficient; it fixes the product. % yield = actual/theoretical × 100.

  1. Explain the mole concept and Avogadro's number. Determine an empirical and molecular formula and solve limiting-reagent problems. [10]

Model answer D1: mole concept, formula determination and stoichiometry (10 marks)

Introduction. One mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 12\ \text{g} of carbon-12, that is N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1} (Avogadro's number). The mass of one mole in grams is the molar mass.

Mole relations.

  1. Number of moles n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{\text{number of particles}}{6.022\times10^{23}}.
  2. For a gas, one mole occupies 22.4\ \text{L} at STP (0^{\circ}\text{C}, 1\ \text{atm}), and 22.7\ \text{L} at 0^{\circ}\text{C}, 1\ \text{bar}.
  3. Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
  4. Law of conservation of mass, law of definite proportions, law of multiple proportions and Gay-Lussac's law of volumes are the laws of chemical combination.

Empirical and molecular formula. The steps are: percentage to mass, mass to moles, divide by the smallest, convert to whole numbers. The molecular formula is n\times the empirical formula, where n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}.

Element % Moles Ratio
C 40.00 3.33 1
H 6.67 6.67 2
O 53.33 3.33 1

The empirical formula is CH₂O (mass 30). With molar mass 180, n = 6 and the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

Limiting reagent. The reactant that is used up first decides the amount of product. For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, take 4\ \text{g} of H₂ (2\ \text{mol}) and 24\ \text{g} of O₂ (0.75\ \text{mol}).

O₂ needs 1.5\ \text{mol} of H₂, so O₂ is limiting. Water formed = 1.5\ \text{mol} = 27\ \text{g} and unused H₂ = 0.5\ \text{mol} = 1\ \text{g}.

Stoichiometry with gases. For CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, 10\ \text{g} of CaCO₃ (0.1\ \text{mol}) gives 0.1\ \text{mol} of CO₂, which is 4.4\ \text{g} or 2.24\ \text{L} at STP. Percentage yield = \dfrac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}}\times100.

Conclusion. The mole links mass, number of particles and gas volume, and the balanced equation gives the mole ratio for every stoichiometry calculation.

Model answer D2: concentration terms and dilution (10 marks)

Introduction. The concentration of a solution tells how much solute is present in a given amount of solution or solvent.

Term Definition Formula Depends on temperature?
Molarity M moles of solute per litre of solution \dfrac{n}{V\ (\text{L})} yes
Molality m moles of solute per kg of solvent \dfrac{n}{W\ (\text{kg})} no
Mole fraction x moles of one component per total moles \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_B} no
Mass percent grams of solute per 100 g of solution \dfrac{w}{W}\times100 no
ppm parts per million by mass \dfrac{w}{W}\times10^6 no
Normality N gram equivalents per litre M\times n\text{-factor} yes

The sum of all the mole fractions is 1. Molality is preferred for physical measurements because it does not change with temperature.

Conversion. For a solution of mass percent w and density d\ (\text{g mL}^{-1}), M = \dfrac{10\,w\,d}{\text{molar mass}}.

Dilution. The number of moles of solute stays constant when water is added: M_1V_1 = M_2V_2. For acid dilution, always add the acid to the water slowly with stirring.

Numerical.

  • Concentrated sulphuric acid is 98\% by mass with d = 1.84\ \text{g mL}^{-1}: M = \dfrac{10\times98\times1.84}{98} = 18.4\ \text{M}.
  • To prepare 250\ \text{mL} of 1\ \text{M} acid: V_1 = \dfrac{1\times250}{18.4} = 13.6\ \text{mL} of the concentrated acid is made up to 250\ \text{mL}.
  • 4\ \text{g} of NaOH in 500\ \text{mL} gives \dfrac{0.1}{0.5} = 0.2\ \text{M}.
  • A solution of 46\ \text{g} ethanol (1\ \text{mol}) in 54\ \text{g} water (3\ \text{mol}): x_{ethanol} = 0.25, x_{water} = 0.75, and the molality is \dfrac{1}{0.054} = 18.5\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}.

Conclusion. Molarity and normality change with temperature while molality and mole fraction do not, and M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 is the key to dilution.
